transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-01
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 62 mins
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lena (Aurora Head of ML), Samir (Platform), Tara (Security), Ben (Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Discussed POC scope for Aurora Finance: load profile, token distributions, latency/cost tradeoffs, and success criteria. Action items: upload logs and run baseline.

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on; quick intro — I'm Maya, AE for Redwood Inference, and Ethan is our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
00:12 Lena: Good, thanks. We're excited to scoping this POC, been looking at your dedicated offering.
00:18 Samir: Yeah quick context — we run a realtime risk scoring microservice that calls models for scoring and explanation. We're mostly throughput sensitive, little bit of latency requirements for UX.
00:30 Maya: Great, that's helpful. The goal today is to nail down workload shape — QPS, concurrency, average and tail token lengths, and define benchmarks and success criteria.
00:45 Ethan: I'll jump in on the technical side. Can you give us typical QPS during peak and concurrency per instance? Also examples of prompt lengths — short, median, and long?
00:58 Ben: Sure — on peak we see about 220 QPS to the scoring endpoint across all regions; concurrency per container roughly 40 active requests, but we batch some requests in the app.
01:10 Lena: Token sizes vary: median input ~ 120 tokens, average output ~ 35 tokens, but we have a long-tail where 5-8% of requests are 800-1500 token prompts for more detailed explanations.
01:27 Tara: From security perspective, all PII is stripped, but we need full audit logs and KMS integration or bring-your-own-key for any production pilot. Also SSO and SAML for console access.
01:42 Ethan: Noted. The long tail will drive KV cache pressure and can increase latency on generation. For the POC we'll want to run a synthetic workload with your token distribution so we can model tail percentiles.
01:57 Maya: What's your latency SLO target for the product? 95th, 99th?
02:02 Samir: For the UI, 95th needs to be under 150ms ideally, 99th under 400ms. For batch scoring (non-UI), we're okay with higher latency but want throughput.
02:15 Ethan: Those are tight numbers — 150ms 95th for generative outputs is aggressive if you have 800-1500 token requests. We should clarify which routes require strict SLOs; perhaps we route long prompts to lower-cost background workers.
02:30 Lena: Right, we already do that in part, but the explainability feature has to be near realtime for support agents. That feature represents about 18% of traffic and contains the long tails.
02:42 Maya: Good — that suggests two-tier POC: a realtime lane targetting <150ms 95th, and a background lane for the rest where throughput/cost are prioritized. The POC should validate both.
02:55 Ben: How do you measure 95th? Per-request end-to-end including network?
03:01 Ethan: We usually measure server-side generation time plus tokenization overhead. For a fair baseline we will run side-by-side tests from your VPC or from dedicated instances and collect network RTT separately.
03:12 Lena: For capacity, what's the conversion from QPS to required GPUs? We have concurrency peaks at ~220 QPS but a lot of those are small prompts — does batching help?
03:24 Ethan: Yes, batchability helps a lot. If most requests are small and can be batched, throughput per GPU goes up. Key variables: average input tokens, output tokens, sequence length during decoding, and whether KV cache hits are common for prefixes.
03:40 Maya: If you can provide token distribution histograms (or even just percentiles), we'll estimate GPU counts and show cost tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated. For POC sizing, we typically run baseline with 2-4 GPUs depending on model size.
03:55 Samir: We can extract anonymized histograms. We'll need a template for the format.
04:02 Maya: We'll send a spreadsheet with buckets: request count, median input tokens, 50/90/95/99 input token sizes, avg output tokens, percent of calls needing explainability.
04:13 Tara: On compliance — SOC2 is a hard requirement for production. For POC, we need to know what logs you retain and access controls. Also, audit logs with user and request IDs for 6 months.
04:26 Ethan: We can provide our SOC2 report and details on audit log retention in the POC environment. For PII, you mentioned stripping — we'll want to confirm. For BYOK, our Private deployment supports KMS/HSM integration.
04:40 Ben: For benchmarking, what's a typical POC run? Duration, what metrics do you capture?
04:46 Ethan: We run two phases: baseline microbench (short runs per model variant) to map latency vs concurrency, then a 2-3 hour stress run with your synthetic traffic to capture tail behavior. Metrics: latency percentiles, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, cost per 1M tokens, error rates, and memory pressure.
05:02 Maya: We'll also include success criteria — e.g., realtime lane 95th < 150ms, error rate < 0.1%, throughput >= 180 QPS for small prompts, and cost offline within defined budget. Is that roughly aligned?
05:16 Lena: Yes, though we might relax throughput to 150 QPS if latency is solid. We need Redwood to propose cost per 1M tokens so we can compare to our current vendor.
05:27 Ethan: We'll produce a model-level cost estimate based on throughput and token distribution; we'll include options: dedicated reserved, burst capacity, or hosted provisioning.
05:36 Maya: Quick note — do you use embeddings for routing or caching? That impacts traffic volume.
05:41 Ben: We use small embeddings for clustering similar tickets; embeddings calls are separate and about 12% of API traffic but are batched in our pipeline.
05:50 Ethan: Good to know. Embedding workload is usually cheaper per-op but can be heavy on throughput. For the POC we'll treat embeddings as a separate workload and outline batching strategies.
06:00 Samir: Timeline question — we want a POC in September, ideally production pilot in October. Is that a realistic schedule?
06:09 Maya: Yes, if we get logs this week and run baseline early next week we can have a results deck by the second week of September. Production pilot in October is realistic pending security signoff and performance.
06:21 Tara: We'll need to review SAML, SOC2, and encryption details before pilot. Expect some legal paperwork for BYOK.
06:28 Ethan: We'll attach our security pack and a sample legal appendix. For BYOK we'll need key rotation windows and KMS endpoints.
06:36 Lena: For the test inputs, do you need raw requests or tokenized versions?
06:40 Ethan: Tokenized distributions help us model exact compute; raw requests are fine, we can tokenize on our side, but if you can give both that'd be ideal.
06:50 Ben: One more practical — are you able to run the POC in our VPC for private deployment? We prefer not to move data to public hosted initially.
06:58 Maya: We support a Private deployment pattern, with control plane access and a customer-managed VPC. For an initial POC we can either run in our dedicated test cluster or spin up a private POC in your account; we'll include both options in the plan.
07:12 Samir: Good. Cost for private POC?
07:15 Ethan: We can do a short-term trial with temporary credits; we'll include a sizing-based cost estimate in the benchmark proposal.
07:22 Maya: Alright let's recap action items — Maya will send benchmark spreadsheet, Ethan will draft test config, Lena will provide anonymized traffic histograms, Tara will confirm compliance needs, and we'll schedule the baseline run week of Sep 6.
07:37 Lena: Sounds good. Thanks all.
07:40 Maya: Thanks folks — we'll follow up by email with docs and calendar invites.
07:44 (call ends)
